1009.title: The universal form
1009.hook: Arjuna asks to see Krishna's true form and is overwhelmed
1009.howItsDone: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita, and the vision of chapter eleven is painted and sculpted as Krishna's universal form, often shown with many heads and arms.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was wajh, the face found wherever you turn. Your line was no turn steps outside it.

Two armies are lined up, ready to fight. Between them sits a chariot with two people in it. One is Arjuna, a warrior who has lost his nerve. The other is his charioteer, Krishna, who has spent a long conversation teaching him. By now Arjuna has heard enough to suspect that his driver is far more than a driver. So he asks: if it's possible, let me see you as you really are. It's a request people make of friends, of lovers, of God. This time, it's granted.
screen: `TWO ARMIES. ONE CHARIOT.` → `LET ME SEE YOU AS YOU ARE.` → `THE REQUEST IS GRANTED.`

segments.voice: This is chapter eleven of the Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture, and it unfolds in four movements. First, the eyes. Krishna tells Arjuna that he can't see this with his ordinary eyes, so he gives him a divine eye, a new way of seeing. Awe here isn't something you squint at; you need different eyes for it. Second, the sight. Arjuna sees the whole universe gathered in one body: countless faces and eyes, ornaments and weapons, the gods themselves, all of it in one form. A narrator reaches for the brightness: if the light of a thousand suns rose in the sky at once, he says, that might come near the splendor of it. Third, the shaking. Arjuna's hair stands on end. He bows his head and folds his hands. As the vision goes on, it turns terrifying: worlds and warriors rushing into blazing mouths like rivers into the sea. Arjuna admits he's lost his bearings and can find no peace. Fourth, the way back. Near the end Arjuna says he's glad to have seen what he had never seen before, and yet his mind is shaken with fear. He asks to see the familiar form again, the one he knows. Krishna gently returns to it, and Arjuna says he is himself again. That's the honesty of this chapter. The vision is real, and it's too much. Hindu readers hear many things here, but the story never pretends that seeing everything is comfortable.
screen: `A DIVINE EYE TO SEE WITH.` · `THE WHOLE UNIVERSE IN ONE FORM.` · `HAIR ON END. NO PEACE.` · `SHOW ME THE FAMILIAR FORM AGAIN.` · then, large: `OVERWHELMED.`

segments.voice: Find the biggest thing you can see from where you are, a long street, a crowd, every leaf on one full tree, and try to take in all of it at once; notice that you can't, and let that be fine. When it gets to be too much, come back to something small and familiar, your hand or the floor, the way Arjuna asked for the form he knew, and then look out again.
Arjuna. The warrior who asked to see Krishna as he really is, and was left overwhelmed by the whole universe in one body. Today's word.
Your line: overwhelmed. Arjuna saw everything, then asked for the face he knew. Day one thousand nine.

1010.title: Not this, not this
1010.hook: the Upanishad describes the ultimate only by saying what it is not
1010.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, teachers use neti neti as a method of inquiry, setting aside the body, thoughts and feelings as 'not this' to point toward the self that observes them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Arjuna, who saw everything at once and asked for the familiar form back. Your line was overwhelmed.

Try describing a silence. You can't say what it sounds like, because it doesn't sound like anything. All you can do is list what's missing: no traffic, no voices, no engine idling down the street. Take enough away, and the other person knows exactly what you mean. One of the Upanishads, the Brihadaranyaka, tries this with the biggest subject of all. It reaches for the ultimate reality, and its answer is two words, said twice.
screen: `DESCRIBE A SILENCE.` → `LIST WHAT'S MISSING.` → `TWO WORDS, SAID TWICE.`

segments.voice: First, the pictures. Before it gets to the two words, the passage pictures the form of the person within, in a run of vivid images: like a saffron-colored cloth, like white wool, like a flame, like a white lotus, like a sudden flash of lightning. Bright, beautiful, quick. Each one catches a glimpse. Second, the turn. Then the text stops and says, in effect: now the teaching. Not this, not this. In Sanskrit, neti neti, a phrase read as two small words run together, na and iti: not thus. All those images were pointing. None of them is the thing. Third, why that isn't a shrug. You might hear not this, not this as giving up. The text hears it the other way: there is nothing higher than this not-this. The refusal is the teaching. Whatever you can picture, point at or put in a sentence is smaller than what the passage is after, so the honest description keeps saying no to every description. Fourth, where it leads. The same passage gives a name for what can't be named: the truth of truth. And some Hindu schools, especially Advaita Vedanta, use neti neti as a practice of the mind. Set aside the body: not this. Set aside the thoughts: not this. Set aside the feelings: not this. What remains when you've said no to everything you can observe, they say, is the one doing the observing. The method is subtraction, all the way down.
screen: `SAFFRON CLOTH, LIGHTNING, A LOTUS.` · `NOW THE TEACHING: NOT THIS.` · `NOTHING HIGHER THAN THIS NOT-THIS.` · `THE TRUTH OF TRUTH.` · then, large: `NETI NETI.`

segments.voice: Let the breath find its own pace, and as each thing arrives, a sound, a thought, a plan, an itch, notice it and say inwardly: not this. You're not pushing anything away, only declining to call it the whole story; between the not-thises, rest in whatever is left. If you pray, the quiet can be your prayer.
Neti neti. Sanskrit for not this, not this: the Upanishad's way of pointing at the ultimate by saying no to every description of it. Today's word.
Your line: the refusal is the teaching. Saffron, wool, flame, lotus, lightning, and then: not this. See you tomorrow.

1011.title: Who really knows?
1011.hook: the Hymn of Creation ends: perhaps even the highest does not know
1011.carry: it ends where it ends, on a question
1011.howItsDone: The Nasadiya hymn (Rig Veda 10.129) is recited in Vedic chanting and studied in Hindu philosophy, where some readers take its closing doubt as a mark of humility before the question of origins.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was neti neti, not this, not this. Your line was the refusal is the teaching.

Where did everything come from? Children ask it at bedtime, and adults ask it at three in the morning. In the Rig Veda, a collection of hymns held sacred in Hindu tradition, a short hymn sets out to answer it too. It's known as the Nasadiya hymn, the Hymn of Creation. It begins in the dark before anything, builds slowly toward the first stirring, and then, at the very end, does something surprising for a hymn. It asks.
screen: `WHERE DID EVERYTHING COME FROM?` → `THE HYMN OF CREATION.` → `AT THE END, IT ASKS.`

segments.voice: First, before the beginning. The hymn opens with a strange double negative: then there was neither what is nor what is not. No air, no sky beyond it. It wonders what covered everything, and where, and whether there was deep water. Death wasn't there, and neither was deathlessness. No sign of night or day. Darkness, it says, was hidden by darkness. Second, the stirring. Into that, something moves. That One, the hymn says, breathed without breath, by its own nature. Desire arose in it, and desire was the first seed of mind. And sages, searching in their hearts, found the tie between what is and what is not. Third, the doubt. Then the hymn turns and asks directly: who really knows? Who here can say where this creation came from? The gods, it points out, came after the creation of the world. So who knows how it arose? Fourth, the ending. The last verse names one possible witness: the one who watches over it from the highest heaven. Surely he knows. And then the final words: or perhaps he does not know. A sacred hymn about the beginning of everything, and its last move is to leave the question standing. Some readers hear humility there. Some hear the edge of what words can do. The hymn itself doesn't say which. It ends where it ends, on a question.
screen: `NEITHER WHAT IS NOR WHAT IS NOT.` · `THAT ONE BREATHED WITHOUT BREATH.` · `THE GODS CAME AFTER.` · `OR PERHAPS HE DOES NOT KNOW.` · then, large: `WHO REALLY KNOWS?`

segments.voice: Choose one question you can't settle, where all this came from, what happens after, why there's anything at all, and ask it once, slowly, inwardly. When an answer starts to form, set it down, the way the hymn sets down its own, and keep the question open, like a door held for someone you can't see yet. If you pray, you can bring the question as it is.
Nasadiya hymn. The Rig Veda's Hymn of Creation, which asks who really knows where everything came from, and closes: perhaps even the one in the highest heaven does not know. Today's word.
Your line: it ends where it ends, on a question. Even the gods, the hymn says, came after. That's day one thousand eleven.

1012.title: The sky as a platter
1012.hook: Guru Nanak's arti: the sky is the platter, sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls
1012.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's arti hymn in the gurdwara, and it is part of Kirtan Sohila, the evening hymns recited before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the Nasadiya hymn, which ends on a question. Your line was it ends where it ends, on a question.

Evening, in a temple. Someone lifts a metal platter of small flames and moves it in slow circles before a sacred image. There may be flowers on the plate, incense in the air, someone waving a fan. This is arti, a ceremony of lamps in Hindu worship. Sikh tradition says that Guru Nanak, the first Sikh Guru, was at a temple during an evening arti like this, and that he lifted his eyes to the sky and sang a hymn. Sikhs still sing it.
screen: `A PLATTER OF SMALL FLAMES.` → `ARTI, A CEREMONY OF LAMPS.` → `GURU NANAK LOOKS UP.`

segments.voice: First, the platter. The hymn, found on page thirteen of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, opens with the sky itself. The sky is the platter. In Gurmukhi: gagan mai thaal. The bowl of the heavens is the plate held up in worship. Second, the lamps. The sun and the moon are the lamps on that platter. The circles of the stars are the pearls scattered across it. In the hymn's picture, the sky is already doing what the worshipers are doing: lifting light. Third, the rest of the ceremony. The fragrance carried down from the sandalwood hills is the incense. The wind is the fan. All the forests and their flowers are the flowers offered. Nothing has to be brought in; the whole creation is already the offering. Then the line that turns it all toward God: what an arti this is, O destroyer of fear. Fourth, the sound. The hymn goes on to say that the unstruck sound, a music no hand plays, is the temple drum. Sikhs sing this hymn in the gurdwara, and it's part of Kirtan Sohila, the hymns recited before sleep. Notice what the hymn doesn't do. It doesn't argue. It widens the frame, until the evening sky is holding up its own lamps to God, and anyone can stand under it.

segments.voice: If it's evening, look out at the sky; if not, close your eyes and remember a sky you've seen at dusk. Find the light that's left, the sun going down, the moon, a first star, and what's moving, the air, a branch, a cloud, and let it all be one slow ceremony that nobody is running. If you pray, let the hymn's words, what an arti this is, rest in you.
Arti. The ceremony of lamps that gave Guru Nanak's hymn its shape: the sky itself as the platter, sun and moon its lamps, stars its pearls. Today's word.
Your line: the sky's arti. Sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls. Day one thousand twelve, done.

1013.title: The river meets the sea
1013.hook: the river god, proud of his flood, reaches the ocean and is humbled
1013.howItsDone: Readers of the Zhuangzi, a classic of Taoist thought, return to the Autumn Floods chapter for its picture of how every point of view is small beside a larger one.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was arti: Guru Nanak's sky as a platter, sun and moon its lamps. Your line was the sky's arti.

It's the season of the autumn floods. Streams from everywhere pour into the Yellow River, and it swells so wide that, standing on one bank, you can't tell an ox from a horse on the other. The god of the river is thrilled. He looks at all that water and decides that every beautiful thing in the world belongs to him. So he sets off downstream, heading east, riding his own current, to see where it goes. That's how the Zhuangzi, a Taoist classic, opens its chapter called Autumn Floods.
screen: `THE AUTUMN FLOODS.` → `CAN'T TELL AN OX FROM A HORSE.` → `THE RIVER GOD IS THRILLED.`

segments.voice: First, the arrival. The river god reaches the North Sea, turns to look east, and can't see where the water ends. All his pride goes out of his face. He sighs to the spirit of the sea and admits it: there's an old saying about someone who has learned a little and thinks nobody can match him, and that, he says, was me. Second, the frog. The sea doesn't scold him. It explains. You can't talk about the ocean to a frog in a well, the sea says: he's stuck in his small space. You can't talk about ice to a summer insect: he's stuck in his one season. The frog isn't foolish. His well is just all he's seen. Third, the opening. Then the sea says the line the whole story turns on: now that you've come out beyond your banks and seen the great sea, you know how small you are, and so now I can talk to you about the great things. The humbling isn't the end of the lesson. It's the door into it. Fourth, the sea's own size. And here's the twist. The sea, which never fills and never runs dry, doesn't think of itself as big either. Next to heaven and earth, it says, I'm like a pebble or a little tree on a great mountain. Every size in this story is real, and every size is small next to a larger one. The river's flood was real. It just hadn't met the sea yet.
screen: `HE CAN'T SEE WHERE THE WATER ENDS.` · `A FROG IN A WELL.` · `NOW I CAN TALK TO YOU.` · `EVEN THE SEA IS A PEBBLE.` · then, large: `THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and call up the biggest water you've ever stood beside: hear it, feel how far it went, and notice your own size next to it, without minding. If a proud thought shows up, a win, a boast, a being-right, let it flow downstream to meet that water. If you pray, you can rest in that wideness.
Autumn Floods. The Zhuangzi chapter where the proud river god reaches the ocean, sees no end to it, and is humbled before he's ready to learn. Today's word.
Your line: the sea. Even the sea calls itself a pebble on a mountain. See you tomorrow.

1014.title: Indra's net
1014.hook: a net of jewels, each reflecting all the others
1014.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers, especially in the Huayan and Zen traditions of East Asia, use Indra's net to teach dependent arising: that each thing exists through its connections to everything else.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Autumn Floods: the river met the sea, and the sea called itself a pebble. Your line was the sea.

At night, a window turns into a mirror. Stand in a lit room and look out, and there you are, with the lamp behind you, and the lamp's reflection in the glass of a picture frame, and the frame in the window too: light bouncing from one surface into the next. Most of the time nobody notices. Buddhist teachers tell of a net that does this on purpose, on a scale with no edges. It hangs over the palace of Indra, a king of the gods in old Indian stories.
screen: `A WINDOW TURNS INTO A MIRROR.` → `LIGHT BOUNCING SURFACE TO SURFACE.` → `A NET OVER INDRA'S PALACE.`

segments.voice: The picture is linked to the Avatamsaka Sutra, a Mahayana Buddhist scripture, and Buddhist teachers have opened it up step by step. First, the net. It stretches out in every direction, with no edge, and at each knot where the threads cross hangs a jewel: clear, polished, shining. Second, the reflection. Look closely into any one jewel, and you'll see in its surface all the other jewels of the net. Not one or two. All of them. Third, the reflection inside the reflection. Each of those reflected jewels is also reflecting all the others. So in the one jewel you're looking at, you see the whole net, and inside every jewel in that picture, the whole net again, without end. One holds all, and all hold the one. Fourth, why the teachers use it. It's a picture of how things are, they say. Nothing exists on its own. Each thing is made of its connections, the way a jewel's whole look comes from what it reflects. Buddhist teaching calls this dependent arising: things come to be because of other things. A modern Zen teacher, Thich Nhat Hanh, gave the idea a plainer name, interbeing, and pointed at a sheet of paper. In it, he said, you can see the tree, the rain, the logger, the sun. Some teachers find a comfort in the net. No jewel is lost in a huge web. Each one is a place where the whole web shows up, the one next to it as much as any.
screen: `A JEWEL AT EVERY KNOT.` · `EACH ONE REFLECTS ALL THE OTHERS.` · `THE NET INSIDE EACH REFLECTION.` · `NOTHING EXISTS ON ITS OWN.` · then, large: `EACH REFLECTS ALL.`

segments.voice: Find something shiny near you, the back of a spoon, a glass of water, a dark screen, and look into its surface without counting: the lamp, a corner of the room, your own face, bent and small. Turn it a little and watch a whole new room slide in, and let it be a jewel in the net, holding everything around it. If you pray, you can give thanks for any of what you see.
Indra's net. A Buddhist image: an endless net with a jewel at each knot, each jewel reflecting all the others. Today's word.
Your line: each reflects all. A jewel at every knot, and the whole net in each. Day one thousand fourteen.

1015.title: The frog and the pond
1015.hook: Basho's haiku: an old pond, a frog jumps in, the sound of water
1015.howItsDone: Readers of haiku read the frog poem slowly and attend to the single moment it records rather than looking for a lesson in it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Indra's net, each jewel reflecting all. Your line was each reflects all. This week: Arjuna overwhelmed, not this, not this, who really knows, the sky's arti, and the sea.

Plop. That's the whole event. A pond that's been sitting there, still, for who knows how long. A frog jumps in. There's a sound, and then the pond is still again. Nothing in that moment would make the news. Nobody would even turn their head. And yet a Japanese poet named Matsuo Basho wrote it down in a single short poem, and made that small sound the whole point. After a week of skies, seas and visions, awe arrives as a splash.
screen: `PLOP.` → `A FROG JUMPS IN.` → `AWE ARRIVES AS A SPLASH.`

segments.voice: Here it is in Japanese: furuike ya, kawazu tobikomu, mizu no oto. In plain English, word for word: old pond. A frog jumps in. The sound of water. First, the old pond. Furuike. Old, still, unremarkable. And then that little word, ya, which works like a pause, a breath held. The poem sets the stillness down first and lets it sit. Second, the frog. Kawazu tobikomu. A frog jumps in. One quick movement. The poem doesn't say what kind of frog, or why it jumped, or whether the poet was startled. Just the jump. Third, the sound. Mizu no oto. The sound of water. Notice where the poem ends. Not on the frog, not on the poet's feelings, not on a lesson. It ends on a sound, and then the poem stops, the way the sound stops, and you're left in the quiet that comes back. Fourth, why it belongs in a stretch about awe. Some readers hear in it the meeting of stillness and motion: the old and unchanging, the sudden and alive, and the moment they touch. Others hear something simpler: pay attention, and the plainest moment is enough. Basho doesn't explain which. The poem gives you no instructions at all. It gives you a pond, a frog and a sound, and trusts you to listen.
screen: `OLD POND, AND A BREATH HELD.` · `A FROG JUMPS IN.` · `IT ENDS ON A SOUND.` · `THE PLAINEST MOMENT IS ENOUGH.` · then, large: `MIZU NO OTO.`

segments.voice: Let the room be the old pond, and wait, without hunting, until a sound comes: a car, a bird, a cough, a door. Meet it the way the poem does, without naming its cause or judging it: hear it arrive, hear it fade, stay for the quiet after, then wait for the next one. If you pray, you can offer the listening itself.
Furuike. Basho's word for the old pond in his poem: a frog jumps in, the sound of water, awe found in the smallest splash. Today's word.
Your line: the sound of water. Old pond, a frog, and then the quiet coming back. And a frog gets the week's last word.
